So our
goal as IPDES is to enable research that contributes to new
discoveries that help address the societal challenges associated with the
biodiversity crisis. The mission is broader than any one infrastructure.
It's about coordinating a globally integrated network of stakeholders and
connecting biodiversity data and knowledge through both technical and social
infrastructure, data, tools, standards, people, and working practices.
This is
a paper that we published four years or so ago now that
kind of builds off of ideas that came out of North America and
Europe around the extended specimen and the digital specimen.
And so we
combined and advanced some of those into the digital extended specimen,
which we feel is a useful way to think about the full ecosystem.
We start with the physical specimen and a digital record, and then the extended
specimen that links that record to additional information and relationships.
And it's a connected architecture, and standards, of course, allow that
information to move easily through these layers.
So when we think about sustainability,
over time and through these various discussions, three major themes
have emerged, three major needs. The first is technology and infrastructure,
and the digital extended specimen can provide a unifying framework for this
very distributed landscape. It helps us identify the critical pieces, understand
how they connect, and demonstrates why sustained investment across those pieces
matters for integrated data and high-impact research.
Another important part is obviously the people.
So,
sustainable infrastructure requires a resilient and inclusive community, supporting
careers and expertise, shared governance, and investment in the people and skills
that actually make the connections work.
We can preserve servers and software, but without the people who understand the
data, standards, collections, and relationships, we haven't preserved the
infrastructure.
And of course, funding, a hot topic on all of our minds always.
Traditional funding sources are increasingly uncertain, so we need to think much
more broadly about the portfolio that supports biodiversity infrastructure,
longer-term public investment, philanthropy, international partnerships, existing
organizations and infrastructures, and potentially new models that recognize the
socioeconomic value created by biodiversity data.
The important point is that sustainability probably won't come from finding one
replacement funding source. It will come from building a more diverse and resilient
model, and we've seen that in various projects and talks, I think, this week
already. So how do we sustain all of this?
